text: A defect free copper interconnect is crucial for ensuring the electrical connection and transmission of high density interconnect printed circuit boards. Leveling agent is a key regulatory factor for achieving dense cop per super filling from bottom to top in blind holes during the electroplating process of high-density interconnect boards. Here, two small molecule five-membered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains, namely 3- amino-5-mercapto-1,2,4-triazole (AMT) and 2–5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT), were selected to be as levelling agents to study their effect on the copper filling behavior on blind holes. Electrochemical tests including cyclic voltammetry solvation (CV) and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) were firstly used to analyze the inhibitory effect of two leveling agents on copper deposition and it was indicated that the MMT has a more significant inhibitory effect on the copper deposition than the AMT. Subsequently, the influence of different concentrations of MMT on the inhibition of copper deposition and the blind hole filling performance were also further analyzed by LSV, CV, and constant current measurement (GM), where an optimal concentration of 7 ppm was obtained for the maximum inhibitory ability on the copper deposition accompanied by the best blind hole filling ability. The characterization analysis from the field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) also illuminates that the MMT leveling agent can effectively reduce the surface roughness of copper filled with micropores and promote the selective growth of copper coatings along the (11 1) crystallographic plane. The adsorption behavior of the levelling agent on the cathode surface during electrodeposition was further also studied by the quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics sim ulations combined with the in situ electrochemical surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy (EC-SERS) experiments. It has been suggested that the thiol, sulfur, and alkyl groups in the leveling agent MMT molecule are nucleophilic groups, providing preferred active sites for adsorption reactions and thus generating effective inhibition ability on copper deposition formation. Thermal shock experiments based on tin immersion showed the copper layer obtained under the addition of the levelling agent MMT has excellent reliability. The comprehensive results indicated that 2-mercapto-5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT) was an effective levelling agent for the blind hole supperfilling.

text: Blind hole copper electroplating is the primary technology used in the connectivity manufacturing process for printed circuit boards (PCB), semiconductor integrated circuit (IC) chips, and IC packaging substrates [1–3]. The issue of achieving complete filling of high-quality plated copper has become increasingly essential in light of the progress made in integrated and miniaturized electronic devices. This is particularly relevant as high-density interconnect printed circuit boards (PCBs) are transitioning towards through-hole and micro-hole designs with larger depth-to-diameter ratios [4]. In the process of copper plating on such PCB micro vias with a larger depth-to-diameter ratio, there is a very significant difference between a current’s density distribution inside and on the surface of the micro vias. In such an environment, the copper electrodeposition rate in the pore area will be significantly greater than that in the micropores’ bottom region, which will result in the coppe layer covering and sealing the pore area in a preferential manner, leading to internal defects in the pores. In order to achieve bottom-up superfilling of the micropores, a synergistic effect of different addi tives is required, namely accelerators, inhibitors, levelling agents and chloride ions. Accelerators are generally small molecule organic sul phides containing specific functional groups of (-S–S-), sulfhydryl (-SH) and sulphonic acid $\left( - S O _ { 3 ^ { - } } \right)$ groups, which typically preferentially adsorb at the micropore’s bottom and can hasten the electrodeposition of copper at the hole’s bottom. SPS and MPS are both common accelerator $[ 5 , 6 ]$ . During copper electrodeposition, the inhibitor is usually adsorbed on the cathode surface and interacts with chloride ions to increase the overpotential, thereby achieving the inhibitory effect on the surface deposition of copper, Inhibitors are mainly macromolecular polyether or polyols [7]. The most prevalent inhibitors are polyethylene glycol (PEG), but in addition to PEG there are also polypropylene glycol (PPG) and triblock copolymers of PEG and PPG [8–10]. Levelling agents can be added in very small amounts compared to inhibitors to achieve a strong inhibiting effect and rapid deactivation, leaving the surface flat and smooth. Meantime, levelling agents also show an inhibiting effect o copper deposition but there is no substitute for inhibitors, which can be compared to short-acting inhibitors, while inhibitors show a moderate inhibiting effect and deactivate slowly, and throughout the plating process, the levelling agent gradually covers the copper surface, domi nating the completion of superconformal deposition [4,7]. Traditiona levelling agents such as Janus Green B (JGB), Diazine Black (DB) Methylene Blue (MB), Alsin Blue (ABPV) [11–14]. However, these dye conventional levelling agents are prone to decomposition at high tem peratures, which makes the plating process not easy to control increasing the cost and also leading to copper plating quality problems. In response to the above problems, researchers have continued t develop new environmentally friendly high-performance small molecul copper plating levelling agents, such as benzyl quaternary ammonium containing compounds phenylacetyl chloride (BZC) [15], 2,2-dithiodi pyridine (DTDP) [16], 4,6-dimethyl-2-mercaptopyrimidine (DMP) [17], tricyclazole (TCA) [18], 1-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-2-tetrazole-5-thion (HPTT) [19]. Synthetic macromolecule polymers such as copolyme synthesized with pyrrole and 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (PBDGE) copolymer, synthesized with imidazole and 1 4-butanediol diglvcidy ether (IBDGE), copolymer synthesized with 1-vinyl imidazole and 1,4 butanediol diglycidyl ether (VIBDGE) [20 22] and so on. These new copper plating levelling agents are phenotyped with good levelling properties. Further studies on the core functional groups and chemica bonds in the leveling agent molecules are needed to investigate thei mechanism of action in the copper electrodeposition process. It has been reported that sulfhydryl groups are the main adsorption sites in com pounds containing sulfhydryl (-SH) functional groups for example Zhao filling of micro via with copper plating. In a previous work, Zhou et al [24] came to the conclusion that the thiadiazol-based main unit com pound 5-amino-1,3,4-thiadiazole-2-thiol could function as an efficien leveling agent and identified the primary adsorption sites as the nitrogen atoms and the side-chain sulfhydryl groups in the thiadiazol ring. Ac cording to the above example, it can be seen that the sulfhydryl (-SH) functional group in the leveling agent molecule is capable of being efficiently absorbed on copper s surface, and nitrogen-nitrogen double bond (-N––N-) and sulfur atoms in the thiadiazol ring have a certain leveling ability. In addition, Hasan F Alesary et al. [25 27] studied the effect of additives on the electrodeposition of metals in deep eutectic solvents (DESs), studied the effect of sodium bromide on the electro deposition of tin, copper, silver and nickel, and found that the curren efficiency of the metal coating was increased when the electrolyte containing sodium bromide was deposited. text: Zn-Ni alloy-modified deep eutectic solvent (DES) was introduced. The electrodeposition of Cu from acetylene 200 DES at 70~^°C with different concentrations of niacin as an additive was studied in detail. So, in the present study, the additives were selected from the point of view of effective functional groups. Two inexpensive, high-performance and environmentally friendly compounds (AMT and MMT) were selected as leveling agents for the screening of small-molecule five-membered heterocyclic compounds. In this paper, two small molecule fivemembered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains, namely 3-amino-5-mercapto-1,2,4-triazole (AMT) and 2-mercapto-5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT), were selected as electroplated copper levelling agents to study their effect on copper deposition and blind hole filling performance, a variety of electrochemical analytical methods including CV, LSV and GM were used to study the inhibitory effect of small molecular five-membered heterocyclic compounds with two different side chains on copper ion deposition and their interaction behavior with other additives. Subsequently, to further study the impact of copper filling blind holes electroplated with MMT acting as a leveling agent, the blind hole filling test was carried out. Thermal shock testing also further verified the reliable performance of the plating. With the help of FE-SEM and XRD, the surface morphology and crystal structure of the copper layer were examined. The investigation focused on the adsorption behavior of MMT molecules at the surface interface using EC-SERS. Furthermore, an investigation was conducted to determine the distribution of the levelling agent on the copper surface and its adsorption capacity. This was accomplished by the utilization of quan tum chemistry calculations and molecular dynamics simulations.

text: The electrochemical tests such as CV, LSV and GM performed in this study were carried out using a rotating disk and a CHI 660C electrochemical workstation. 250 ml of plating solution in a glass container and room temperature electrochemical tests were performed. The threeelectrode test system employed had a platinum rotating disc electrode (Pt-RDE) with a 5 mm diameter as the working electrode (WE), a saturated calomel electrode as the reference electrode (RE) and a platinum wire electrode as the counter electrode (CE). text: There are two types of PCBs, each with a different size blind hole (the hole size and depth were 120 μm x75 μm and 100 μm x 125 μm, respectively) were employed in the blind hole electroplating filling experiment. Before electroplating, the copper plate containing 0.0 4 % ~ 0.065 % phosphorus is wrapped in a filter bag as the anode, and the surface oxide of the copper plate containing phosphorus is polished off with 1000 mesh and 2000 mesh sandpaper before use. After rinsed off the sanding with deionized water, the surface oxide is activated with 1 mol/L sulfuric acid for 3 min, and the surface oxide is completely removed. text: Conventional Raman spectroscopy (Raman) was performed on a solid leveler (MMT) sample pressed on a slide using a Horiba LabRAM HR Raman spectrometer model with a power of 0.625 Mw and an excitation wavelength of λ=633 nm, and the EC-SERS using a Horiba LabRAM. The working electrode was a 6 mm copper electrode, the reference electrode utilized in the experiment was a mercury oxide electrode, while the counter electrode employed was a platinum wire electrode. Prior to the measurement, the working electrode was first polished to a mirror finish with metallurgical sandpaper and \tt α · \tt Al_2 \tt O_3 polishing powder (1, 0.3 and 0.05 µm), from coarse to fine. The test device underwent ultrasonication in ultrapure water for a duration of ten minutes, followed by thorough rinsing with ultrapure water. Subsequently, the equipment was subjected to drying in an oven and subsequently set aside. The electrochemical Raman cell, electrodes, solution bottle and peristaltic pump were assembled together through Teflon tubing in turn, the peristaltic pump was turned on to control the flow rate of the solution, and the air in the electrochemical Raman cell was drained and ensured to be filled with the solution, then the electrochemical Raman cell was placed horizontally on a carrier table and connected to an electrochemical workstation, and a laser source was illuminated vertically on the surface of the electrodes, and a constant current of 1.5 ~A/dm2 was applied by turning on the electrochemical workstation and applying a constant current of 1.5 A/dm2. During the experiment, in order to enhance the Raman signal, the concentration of the base plating solution was reduced in the same proportion ( 2.2 ~\g/ LCuSO _4·5H_2O+ 0.5 5g/LH_2SO_ 4), and the concentration of the additive MMT was 0.1 g / L, and at the same time, the Raman laser intensity is increased to 100 % to improve the signal intensity of the Raman spectrum, and then the signal acquisition was carried out to study the adsorption of additives on copper surfaces in the process of plating through the change of the characteristic peaks of the levelling agent in the Raman signal.

text: First, using cyclic voltammetric stripping, which was carried out in a base solution with SPS and PEG, SPS, PEG, and MMT/AMT, respectively, at two rotational speeds of 100 rpm and 1600 rpm, the effect of two types of five-membered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains on the electrodeposition behavior of copper was investigated. The findings are depicted in Fig. 2. The observation of Fig. 2 reveals that the dissolution peaks of copper obtained from electroplating solutions containing two kinds of small molecule five membered heterocyclic compounds additives are significantly smaller than those obtained from the base plating solution whether at the 100 rpm or at the 1600 rpm. The results of the aforementioned inquiry suggest that the introduction of two small molecules consisting of five-membered heterocyclic compounds can effectively enhance cathodic polarization and prevent the deposition of copper. Moreover, it was further observed that the copper dissolution peak was smaller when 5 ppm MMT was added than when 5 ppm AMT was added. This means that the additive MMT is superior to AMT in inhibiting copper deposition through levelling agents.

text: To find out the inhibitory impact of MMT at the ideal concentration on copper deposition in blind holes’ bottoms and surfaces (i.e., in the strong convection environments and the weak convection intensity), here CV and LSV experiments were also further performed at two different rotational speeds to analyze the differences in the inhibitory behavior of MMT with the optimal concentration on the copper deposition. Fig. 6 shows the cyclic voltammetric dissolution curves for 7 ppm MMT at different speeds. As shown in the figure, the peak of copper dissolution under strong convection (i.e., at 1600 rpm) conditions is significantly smaller than that under weak convection conditions (i.e., at 100 rpm). This indicates that the magnitude of convective significantly influences the inhibitory efficacy of MMT additives on the process of copper electrodeposition; the stronger the convection, the greater the inhibitory ability of MMT on copper deposition. The efficacy of the MMT additive to suppress copper deposition is dependent on its convective strength, as demonstrated by the LSV experimental results presented in Fig. 7. As depicted in Fig. 7, Copper’s deposition potential obtained from the optimum concentration of MMT plating solution under strong convection conditions was significantly shifted in a more negative direction as compared to the copper deposition potential under a weak convection environment, which indicates that MMT has a stronger ability to inhibit copper deposition under strong convection environment. According to previous reports [29–31], such strong convection dependent suppression behavior is suitable for bottom-up electroplated copper overfilling of blind holes.

text: To further demonstrate MMT’s levelling ability and the impact of its addition concentration on the effect of blind hole super-filling copper, two types of PCB boards with varying blind hole sizes were utilized. (i.e., 75 μm x 120 μm and 125 μm x 100 μm in depth and width, respectively) also used here to carry out blind hole filling copper tests. The current density is set to $1 . 5 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ . Fig. 9 shows the cross-sectional view of blind hole filling copper at different concentrations of MMT. As shown in Fig. 9(a) without the addition of the leveling agent MMT, there are large defects inside the blind holes. With the additive MMT added to the plating solution for plating, the findings are shown in Fig. 9 (b-g). From ${ \mathrm { F i g . ~ } } 9 \left( \mathbf { b } \right) ,$ , when 1 ppm MMT is applied the blind holes have a tendency to be filled from the bottom up although there are still large defects inside the blind holes. From Fig. 9 (c), when 2 ppm is added, the filling from the bottom up is more obvious. From Fig. 9 (e), with 5 ppm addition, the blind holes are basically filled without defects. As depicted in ${ \mathrm { F i g . ~ } } 9 \left( \mathbf { f } \right) ,$ , when 7 ppm is added, the perfect filling of the blind hole is realized. As shown in Fig. 9 (g), when 9 ppm MMT was added, pore defects appeared inside the blind hole, which may be related to competitive adsorption. Excessive MMT not only forms adsorption on the surface of PCB blind holes but also diffuses into the interior of the blind holes, leading to an imbalance between accelerators and inhibitors inside the holes, resulting in a stronger inhibitory effect on copper deposition inside the holes, thereby affecting the acceleration effect of SPS. In conclusion, it can be shown that 7 ppm MMT as levelling agent can achieve perfect filling of blind holes. Similarly, plating experiments were carried out in blind hole sizes with higher depth to width ratio (1.25:1), as shown in Fig. 10 (a-f), and plating was carried out with the addition of 7 ppm MMT, and Fig. 10 depicts the plating results and demonstrates that flawless filling of blind holes is still possible at larger depth to width ratios.

text: At the same time, blind hole plating experiments were carried out under the same conditions using AMT as a levelling agent and the corresponding plating results are shown in Figs. 11 and 12, respectively. Subsequently, the obtained plated filled PCB boards were also immersed in molten tin for thermal stress testing to further investigate the reliability of the blind hole copper plating layer obtained under the optimum formulation system. The results are shown in Fig. 13. As shown in Fig. 13, the copper layer in the blind holes did not show any delamination, hole wall sep aration or fracture after several immersion tests in tin. This indicate that the copper layer plated under the optimum formulation system meets the practical needs.

E LUMO closely related to the molecule’s ability to accept electrons and E_HOMO to the molecule’s correlates with the ability to give electrons [16]. text: 4. Conclusion
text_index: 4. Conclusion
raw: 4. Conclusion

text: In summary, two small five-membered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains, namely AMT and MMT, were selected as electroplated copper levelling agents in this paper. The electrochemical anal ysis of CV, LSV, and GM showed that MMT has greater inhibitory ability in inhibiting copper deposition behavior compared to AMT. An optima concentration (7 ppm) of MMT added for effectively suppressing copper deposition was obtained by electrochemical analysis from the CV, LSV, and GM experiments based on the addition of different concentrations of MMT additives. The blind hole filling experiment further demonstrates that such an optimal addition concentration for MMT can achieve cop per overfilling in high aspect ratio PCB blind holes. Characterization analyses from FE-SEM, AFM, and XRD also further demonstrate that the coating obtained at this optimal concentration of MMT has the densest and smoothest surface with a typical 111 texture preferential growth. The thermal shock experiment based on tin immersion indicates that the copper layer obtained using MMT as a leveling agent has good reli ability. It is indicated by in-situ Raman spectroscopy analysis that the adsorption of MMT molecules on the electrode surface is a time dependent process and the C–S, C–N, N––N, and - CH bonds are preferentially adsorbed on the electrode surface. The smaller energy gap value (ΔE = 3.729 (ev)) for the MMT molecule calculated by quantum chemistry further indicates that suggest that the MMT molecules have strong adsorption capacity. Furthermore, Quantum chemical calcula tions based on the electronic potential energy of the MMT molecula structure indicate that the thiol group, sulfur bond, and alkyl groups from the MMT molecular belong to nucleophilic groups and provides the preferred adsorption reaction active sites for interaction with the copper surface, which is consistent with the results from the in situ electrochemical enhanced Raman spectroscopy. The adsorption of these nucleophilic groups on the copper surface effectively inhibits copper deposition and thereby achieving bottom-up copper overfilling in blind holes. These results from the electrochemical analysis and theoretical calculations fully demonstrate that MMT is an effective levelling agent for PCB blind hole filling.
